newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition calls for union support.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition calls for union support.

text.p: Serbia's opposition said on Thursday it planned to draw trade unions into a wave of unrest, openly declaring it hoped to sweep President Slobodan Milosevic from power.

A column of opposition supporters estimated to be more than 80,000-strong again marched through the centre of Belgrade, in the latest of a series of daily protests that made their way through the streets past the symbols of Milosevic's power.
Belgrade residents leaned from their apartments overlooking the march, making a Serbian three-fingered salute and cheering the opposition leaders at the head of the crowd.
The demonstrations began when local authorities overturned most opposition victories in municipal elections held on November 17.
But the opposition Zajedno coalition, which claimed to have won 15 of Serbia's 18 biggest towns said the demonstrations were now aimed at toppling Milosevic.

Serbia's Association of Independent Trade Unions, which says it represents 700,000 workers, issued a call to its members to join the protest. Chairman Dragan Milovanovac said it was possible a strike would be called from Monday.

"The regime is very afraid of workers," he told Reuters. "It is the old communist conviction that when workers go out on the streets it is the end and they are now trying in every possible way (to prevent that)."
One of the Zajedno leaders, flamboyant writer Vuk Draskovic, embraced a tram driver who stopped his tram and rang its bell in support of the protesters.
"I welcome you to our ranks, and I hope all your colleagues will follow your lead," he told the driver before television cameras.
Another opposition leader, Zoran Djindjic, acknowledged they needed union support if they were to succeed in ousting Milosevic and said harnessing it would not be easy.
"The state has a well entrenched system in place that prevents strikes," he said.
Workers from industrial towns that traditionally supported the Socialists have joined other opposition rallies, but Milosevic still has a core of loyal union members.
Despite the deteriorating winter weather, the opposition has consistently summoned crowds of between 50,000 to 100,000.
Before Thursday's march, Draskovic appealed for calm to avoid a repetition of the previous day's scenes when protesters smashed plate glass windows at state television and newspaper offices.
The 700-metre long column of opposition supporters again pelted the buildings with eggs and firecrackers for a third day running, but the damage was limited to egg stains.
Earlier Western human rights groups joined Zajedno in protesting against what they say are attempts by the authorities to silence independent media.

The capital's only independent radio station, B-92, said its signal was jammed every time it attempted to broadcast news. Journalists walked out of another newspaper complaining of editorial censorship under pressure from the authorities.
Milosevic brutually crushed similar protests in 1991 with tanks and water cannon. This time he faces demonstrations in several other towns across the country.
Large numbers of workers have joined rallies in Kragujevac and Nis, industrial towns that were once Milosevic strongholds.

Re-run elections took place on Wednesday in cities where results 10 days ago were overturned. Despite an opposition-led boycott in Belgrade, state media reported the Socialists had secured enough seats to form a majority.
